questions.topic: Margin of error and sample size
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the margin of error changes as sample size grows
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer measures the brightness of 400 stars in a nearby open cluster with a homemade photometer and wants to quote a margin of error for the mean magnitude.

options.text: Doubling the number of star measurements shrinks the margin of error by roughly the square root of two
Doubling the number of star measurements halves the margin of error because precision rises with effort
options.misconception: Believes precision improves in direct proportion to sample size

options.text: Doubling the number of star measurements leaves the margin of error unchanged because it is fixed
options.misconception: Assumes only instrument calibration sets the error

options.text: Doubling the number of star measurements removes the margin of error entirely from the estimate
options.misconception: Assumes more data eliminates uncertainty altogether

questions.explanation: The standard error of a mean falls with the square root of n, so twice the measurements shrink the interval by about 1.41. Halving it outright overstates the gain and removing it entirely ignores instrument scatter.
questions.hint: Think about the square-root rule for a standard error.

options.text: The scale cannot register galaxies dimmer than seventh magnitude, so the ratings are bunched at the top

options.misconception: Believes more observations fix a ceiling in the rating scale

options.text: The ratings are unreliable because the observer recorded them on a nine-point scale
options.misconception: Assumes the problem lies in the number of scale points used

questions.explanation: Because the instrument cannot register values below its floor, ratings cluster at the top and no true differences appear. The fix is a scale with more headroom, not more raters or more scale points.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: State what a defensible sample size plan must contain
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer must survey 1000 galaxies in a nearby cluster and write a plan explaining why a sample of 250 star fields is enough to estimate the mean magnitude within 0.2 magnitudes.

answer.exemplar: A plan should state the target population, the desired margin of error, and the assumed variability of stellar magnitude, then show how the calculated sample size of 250 fields reaches that margin of error. questions.explanation: A defensible plan links the desired precision to variability and shows the calculation itself. Stating a target margin without showing the arithmetic leaves the sample size as an unjustified number.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a saturated reading destroys the information a measure exists to capture
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's brightness scale tops out at magnitude 6, so every star brighter than that reads as exactly 6.0. Explain why this makes the instrument useless for studying a bright cluster.

answer.exemplar: The instrument cannot distinguish among stars at or above the ceiling, so all of them produce the identical reading and the observed variation collapses to zero. Any analysis of brightness trends on this cluster is therefore driven by measurement limits and the recorded spread badly understates the real spread.

questions.explanation: A ceiling flattens real differences into a single value, destroying the variation the instrument exists to capture. The fix must extend the instrument's range; more repeats of an already saturated reading add nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what a saturated reading does to the observed spread.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why adding a modest number of observations cannot halve the margin of error
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer wrote that adding 100 more star measurements to a survey of 400 would halve the uncertainty in the mean magnitude. Explain why that claim is wrong.

answer.exemplar: The standard error of a mean falls with the square root of the sample size, so going from 400 to 500 measurements multiplies it by the square root of 400 over 500, roughly 0.89. That is only about an 11 percent improvement, so the uncertainty is far from halved; halving the margin of error would need four times as many measurements.

questions.explanation: Uncertainty falls with the square root of n, so 400 to 500 measurements improves the margin by roughly a ninth. Halving the margin of error would require quadrupling the sample, not adding a quarter more.
questions.hint: Compare 400 and 500 under the square-root rule.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why stratification suits a population with a rare subgroup
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer has two clean galaxies and hundreds of faint ones in a cluster. Explain why a stratified design is likely to serve the survey better than pure simple random sampling here.

answer.exemplar: A simple random sample would include mostly the numerous faint galaxies, since they outnumber the bright ones, so the rare bright targets would be represented only occasionally and the sample would need to be very large to capture them. Stratifying by brightness class and sampling within each class guarantees the bright galaxies appear, giving more balanced coverage of the cluster with a smaller overall sample.

questions.explanation: With hundreds of faint galaxies and only two bright ones, simple random sampling would usually miss the bright pair. Stratifying by brightness class guarantees each class is represented without inflating the whole sample.
questions.hint: Compare expected class counts under chance versus strata.

answer.exemplar: The atlas lists only northern galaxies, so the southern half of the straddling cluster has no entry and therefore no chance of being selected. options.text: Measure more stars in each group, since the standard error of the difference shrinks with n

questions.explanation: Detectability depends on the standard error of each mean, which falls with the square root of the number of independent stars. Repeating the same stars adds no independent units, so the gain is small.
questions.hint: Ask what counts as an independent unit of information.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a clustered sample shows a larger standard error
questions.stem: A club surveys 400 members using simple random sampling and another 400 using cluster sampling by meeting night. The cluster version's estimated standard error is larger. Why is that expected?

options.text: The cluster sample used older membership records, which are always noisier
options.misconception: Blames record age rather than the correlation within clusters

options.text: Members at the same meeting share views, so the cluster sample contains less independent information
The cluster sample covered the whole club, so it had to include unusual members
options.misconception: Treats wider coverage as the source of extra error

options.text: The two samples had the same design effect, so the difference came from the standard error
options.misconception: Confuses the design effect with the standard error itself

questions.explanation: Members at the same meeting are not independent, so each added member adds less new information and the standard error stays larger. This inflation of variance is exactly the design effect.
questions.hint: Think about whether members at one meeting are independent.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Derive the number of sites a fixed budget can fund
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's survey has a fixed budget of 1,200 and each remote site costs 400 in travel and setup, yielding 25 measurements. Explain how many sites can be funded and what that implies for the total measurements.

answer.exemplar: With 1,200 available and 400 per site, the survey can fund three sites, which between them yield 75 measurements. The tempting move is to spread the budget across six cheaper sessions, but the cost per site is fixed, so cutting the number of sites cuts the yield faster than it saves money, and the survey ends up with far fewer measurements than its size suggests.

questions.explanation: Three sites at 400 each fit the 1,200 budget, and three sites at 25 measurements give 75 measurements. The tempting error is to read a smaller spend per visit as a higher yield, ignoring the fixed cost per site.
questions.hint: Divide the budget by the fixed cost of one site.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of a frame left out of a sample
questions.stem: A frame lists 5,000 galaxies and a survey takes a 0.5 percent sample. How many galaxies are selected, and how many members of the population are left out of the sample entirely?
questions.explanation: Half a percent of 5,000 is 25 galaxies selected, so 5,000 minus 25 leaves 4,975 galaxies outside the sample. The size of that omitted group is what a reader needs to judge the survey's coverage.
questions.hint: Take the sampling fraction, then subtract from the frame size.
